lesson: Paint the change; do not cut and shift the part. When a sprite part must open or close inside an existing outline (a mouth, an eye), keep the original pixels in place and paint the change within the outline — for a mouth, grow a dark wedge downward from the closed mouth line, hinged at the jaw corner, clip inner detail (tongue) inside the wedge, and clip everything to the foreground silhouette. A cut-and-shifted segment leaves a doubled outline and a smeared, speckled edge that survive later patch fixes. Basis: in the 2026-10-26 wolf face GIF, the translated chin produced exactly those two defects; they were found only by a full-resolution, frame-by-frame comparison against the original after Fujii's second correction, and the paint-only redesign removed the whole defect class because no seam can exist. Limit: this covers changes expressible as interior growth or darkening within an existing outline. Articulated limbs still need segmentation, with joint caps and the same full-resolution verification.

lesson: Never overwrite a delivered filename. A revision delivered under the same name may never reach the receiver: the client can keep showing a cached older version while the file on disk is already new, and the receiver will rightly report that the change 'is not there'. Allocate every delivered revision a fresh versioned name, <slug>_vNNN.<ext> with NNN = the largest existing version for that slug + 1, zero-padded; let the build script allocate it and assert the target does not exist. Basis: on 2026-10-26 the hinomaru-eye GIF was correct in the file (verified pixel by pixel) while Fujii's app still showed the older blue-eyed version; on 2026-10-27 Fujii marked this 'super important' and directed that it be prevented by a mechanism, elegantly using numbers, not by a promise (his words: 絶対に、こうならない仕組む、例えば、番号等を上手くエレガントに工夫して、活用して下さい！). Limit: versioned names guarantee that no existing delivered file is overwritten; they cannot force every client to refresh, so the new name itself is the delivery mechanism.

lesson: One mechanism per effect. If two mechanisms produce the same visible effect, they will overlap, read as a defect, and make tuning ambiguous; remove the redundant one instead of coordinating both. Basis: the wolf GIF had a long closed-eye stretch during the howl (driven by the swell curve) and, added later, a blink — two different ways of closing the eye. Fujii identified the overlap and directed that the closed-eye part be deleted; the eye is now always open and the blink (twice per cycle, ~0.24s each) is the only closing event, which also simplified the parameter sheet (the slow eye curve was abolished). This is an instance of the standing keyword エレガント in the programming sense: simple, non-redundant design. Limit: a distinct expressive state (sleeping, stunned) is a different effect, not an overlap; judge by effect, not by part.

lesson: When auditing herd sprites under the design law, read the AI layer in two tiers before judging elements. Tier 1, the signature system, is derived from the member's own trait and serves its skill — the two-question test applies in full and the deformation budget belongs here. Tier 2, the revival chassis (the shared grey-module and AI-Blue-node house style), means membership itself — 'this being was revived by AI, 0 to 1' — and is judged by a different test: is it quiet, consistent, and not competing with the signature for the eye? A chassis element that shouts is audited as a signature. Re-derivation must stay honest: mark confidence per element (elephant feet genuinely sense ground vibration, so the mammoth's leg bands re-derive strongly; the archaeopteryx head orb's 'translation interface' story is the weakest and may be retrofit), never let an invented story launder a decoration, and leave every verdict to Fujii's eye. The design principles fixed from this definition for the experiment lane (stored 2026-10-30)

lesson: In Ark Project terms, card-making (カード化) is fundamentally interactive fun: the world changes in response to taps and sliders. A card is not a board that carries a record (a specimen label) but a small world that responds to the reader's finger. This is not decoration but honesty to the content: the hypothesis itself is a verb (probability to certainty, 0 to 1), and each species' story is a change (collapse, transformation, silencing) — a static medium can only state change, an interactive one can enact it, making the reader an executor of the hypothesis. The reader's journey is: be surprised, touch, watch the world change, ask why, then reach the extinction record on their own — play is the entrance, the record is the main text, and a direction children delight in is the sensitivity gauge for whether the essence landed. Corollaries Fujii set the same day: judge experiments by whether the essence lands, not by polish; bugs are fine because failure IS Bottleneck detection — execute proactively in the experiment lane, map bottlenecks, feed them into the Feedback/correction cycle. Two-lane discipline makes the proactivity safe: the canonical deck is protected (versioned, never overwritten, sprites untouched without Fujii's eye) while the experiment lane is free to break.

Generation variance is not error but a motion resource: near-identical generated variants of one state form animation frames (paper-theater / persistence of vision). Production rule derived 2026-10-30: keep STATES at +1 (one turning point per card) and multiply FRAMES around that state; vary exactly ONE axis per frame set — measured evidence: the three howling-wolf candidates varied independently on head-raise (peak in candidate C) and ring spread (peak in B), with pairwise pixel diffs of 9.4–12.9, so they form an edited composite rather than a clean phase sequence. Robust method: generate a surplus, measure frame differences, select the set that sits evenly inside the motion band, and register frames by foreground bounding box before sequencing. Canonized as DESIGN-LAW v003 §6.7; the value gate for such animation (user operation only) is DESIGN-LAW v003 ch.7.
